questions.q: Define "protagonist" and name the protagonist of each of the four stories in this chapter.
questions.a: A protagonist is the central character who drives the narrative's primary conflict and undergoes the most significant change or revelation. The four protagonists are: the King (इगपुकु), कसज (कसज), the Fairy Queen (पक्ज गकफक), and the Donkey (लक>क). A wrong answer (e.g., naming the narrator of "कसज" as protagonist) reveals confusion between narrative perspective and narrative centrality — a frequent board error where students equate "most pages" with "protagonist."

questions.q: Using the King in "इगपुकु," explain the difference between a flat and a round character. Is the King flat or round? Justify with two textual details.
questions.a: A flat character embodies a single trait and does not change; a round character displays complexity, contradictions, and development. The King is round: his decrees escalate from ears to thoughts (showing paranoid progression), and his final isolation — ministers blindfolded, unable to see each other — reveals systemic collapse stemming from his psychology. A wrong answer calling him "flat because he is a symbol" misses that his psychological escalation (ear → eye → tongue → thought) constitutes character development, not mere allegory.

questions.q: Read this new paragraph: "The village headman announced a new tax. The farmers whispered but paid. Next month he doubled it. The farmers sold jewelry. The third month he demanded their sons. The farmers sharpened ploughshares." Identify two traits of the headman with one piece of evidence each.
questions.a: Trait 1: Exploitative — "doubled it" after initial compliance shows escalating greed. Trait 2: Blind to consequences — "demanded their sons" ignores the breaking point. Steps: (1) Highlight actions (announced, doubled, demanded), (2) Infer motive from escalation, (3) Quote exact phrases as evidence. A wrong answer writing "he is bad" without textual quotes reveals reliance on telling, not showing — a marking-scheme penalty in board exams.

questions.q: Compare how each protagonist relates to authority: the King (holds it), कसज (embodies mysterious authority), the Fairy Queen (exercises bureaucratic authority), the Donkey (submits to authority). What pattern emerges about the author's view of power?
questions.a: The King's authority is performative and collapses internally; कसज's is mystical and unchallenged until he chooses to leave; the Fairy Queen's is procedural and fails until magic intervenes; the Donkey's is absent — he is acted upon. The pattern: authority in these stories is either theatrical (King, Queen), inexplicable (कसज), or imposed (Donkey). No protagonist wields legitimate, stable power. A wrong answer treating all four as "powerful characters" misses the satirical differentiation — a key competency for case-based questions.

questions.q: Which protagonist most effectively critiques societal power structures? Defend your choice using evidence from two stories.
questions.a: The King in "इगपुकु" is most effective. His decrees (ears → eyes → tongues → thoughts) satirize the totalitarian impulse to colonize inner life. The ministers' blindfolded helplessness proves the system destroys its own enforcers. In contrast, the Fairy Queen's bureaucracy ("experts signed contracts") mocks administrative theater but resolves magically, softening the critique. The King's deadpan realism makes the horror mundane — a sharper societal mirror. A wrong answer choosing कसज because "he is mysterious" confuses thematic intrigue with structural critique.

questions.q: Write a 50-word diary entry from the Donkey's perspective the night after the vulture episode, revealing his internal conflict without summarizing the plot.
questions.a: A strong entry uses first-person voice, sensory detail ("feathers brushing my flank"), references the vulture's exclusion ("तुम्हारा कोई अधिकार नहीं"), and expresses yearning for the old group ("crow's caw felt like home"). It shows, not tells, vulnerability. A poor entry writes: "Today the vulture said I can't graze with them. I felt sad. Then a mediator made us eat together." This summarizes plot instead of voicing interiority — a common board-exam weakness in creative-response questions.
